team_results.recap: Detroit led 21-0 before New Orleans — as the flagged depleted secondary and 49.5 total both foreshadowed — stormed back to tie it 24-24 late in regulation, forcing overtime. Jahmyr Gibbs (3 TD, 156 yards) and a Goff-to-St. Brown OT score pulled out a 31-30 win after New Orleans' 2-point try for the outright win failed. The Skeptic's secondary-depletion flag was directionally right even though DET escaped with the pick intact.

Dallas lost 28-20 at the Giants despite entering as road favorites; the Skeptic's rebuttal — that the rebuilt post-Parsons-trade defense was a real liability, not added strength — played out as New York piled up 394 total yards to Dallas's 244 and controlled the game with an 8-minute third-quarter drive.

Tennessee was outgained 361-195 and held to a garbage-time touchdown in a 23-10 loss to the Jets, whose defense limited Cam Ward to 140 yards passing and 68 rushing yards allowed. It's the Titans' sixth straight season-opening loss.

The Jets beat Tennessee 23-10, outgaining the Titans 361-195. QB Justin Fields/OC Frank Reich's offense scored on an opening 8-play drive and the defense limited Cam Ward to 140 yards passing behind a strong Aaron Glenn-coached unit in year two.

The Giants beat Dallas 28-20 on Sunday Night Football, John Harbaugh's debut win, behind Jaxson Dart (230 yards passing, 3 TD, 0 INT, plus 54 rushing yards) and a 394-244 total-yardage edge. Dart became the first QB in NFL history to open a season with 3 pass TD, 50+ rush yards, and a 130+ rating — the pregame 'unproven Dart/Skattebo combo' negative didn't hold up at all.

Arizona's stunning 26-14 win — Jacoby Brissett throwing for 277 yards/1 TD, Trey McBride going for 95 yards/1 TD, rookie HC Mike LaFleur winning his debut — was the NFL's biggest Week 1 upset, coming from the week's single lowest win probability on the board (14%).

lessons_learned.lesson: A trap flag backed by a concrete, quantifiable signal (reverse line movement plus a specific personnel weakness — LAC's OL/QB mobility issues) called the week's biggest upset correctly, while a trap flag built mainly on narrative (JAX's 'post-breakout letdown' and 'new DC is unknown' framing, with no concrete weakness identified) was a clean false alarm. Weight trap flags toward cases with at least one hard, checkable signal (line movement, a specific missing/injured starter) over pure storyline/vibes-based reasoning.

The no-lazy-favorite policy passed its first live test: the excluded largest Vegas favorite (LAC, 85% raw implied) suffered the week's biggest upset loss while the recommendation that went to the next-best team (DET) won, saving a pick outright. This is early evidence (n=1 week) that the policy's premise — the single largest raw-ML favorite is exactly where market/public overconfidence is most likely to get punished — has real teeth, not just theoretical justification. Continue applying it without softening.

The archived Week 1 board (data/history/week_analysis_2026_wk01.json) was missing entries for 4 of the week's 32 teams (SEA, NE, LA, SF — the SEA@NE and LA@SF games), even though every other game's both sides were represented. Future survivor-pick runs should verify all 32 teams for the week appear in the board before archiving/overwriting — a missing team can't be graded later and silently shrinks the calibration sample.

Apply L1's hard-signal-over-narrative rule to the OPPONENT's weaknesses too, not just to trap flags. Week 2's recommendation (TB, 0.76) lost to a CLE team whose low number rested mostly on narrative: fan revolt, QB-benching rumors, and a months-old Garrett trade that was already priced in. Meanwhile the teams discounted for confirmed, current multi-starter injury clusters (BAL, LAC) both lost. When a pick's case is mainly 'the opponent is a mess,' the Skeptic should require concrete, current evidence (injury report, efficiency data) of that mess. Otherwise the Arbiter should pull the number back toward the market or below it.

Teams pulled onto the shortlist only because of a large raw moneyline gap, despite weak own-team form, went 0-2 in Week 2 (TB -6.0 pd/g in Week 1, lost to CLE; LAC -12.0 pd/g, lost to LV). A team whose own recent point differential is poor should not jump straight to #1 recommendation on the matchup gap alone. Treat its weak own-form metrics as a real negative in the debate instead of explaining them away, and be especially wary when it is only a late addition to the shortlist.

Reverse line movement caused by a starting-QB injury is not a trap signal by itself. That news is already fully priced into the moved line, so it is not hidden sharp skepticism. SEA's flag (Darnold out, ~6-7 pt move) was a clean false alarm: backup Drew Lock beat a weak division rival 31-7 in Seattle's 10th straight win in the series. Flag QB-out spots only when the drop-off meets an opponent capable of exploiting it, and check the series/matchup history before calling a trap. BAL's validated flag, by contrast, rested on a broad multi-position injury cluster plus a hot opposing offense.

Favorites priced up mainly because the OPPONENT's starting QB is out went 1-2 in Week 3: PHI lost 27-7 to CHI's third-stringer Keenum, SEA lost 33-31 to WAS backup Mariota, and only SF beat Brissett. Add Week 2's TB loss to a 'mess' CLE team and the pattern holds. Experienced veteran backups (Keenum, Mariota, Brissett) playing at home are not a big drop-off. Once the market has moved the line for the QB news, don't stack a further discount on the opponent for it. Treat it as already priced, and grade the favorite on its OWN health and form. This extends L4/L6.

When the Skeptic's hard signal is a specific missing position group that lines up with what the opponent does well (SEA without both starting safeties vs. a WAS passing attack, on a 2nd straight East road trip), the Arbiter should not call it a wash just because the opponent's injury list is longer. Weigh injuries by matchup relevance, not by count: SEA at 0.72 lost, while the longer WAS injury list didn't matter. Similarly, SF's thinned pass rush let Brissett throw for 280 yds in a closer-than-expected game. The haircut on SF was correct, and a larger one on SEA was warranted.

Severe weather (heavy rain, ~40-mph gusts) suppresses BOTH offenses, so it compresses scoring and favors the side with the better defense and kicking. It does not specifically help an opponent exploit the favorite's backup QB. NYG's weather-amplified trap flag was a false alarm (won 12-7 on four FGs while TEN nearly had no first down by halftime). Don't count bad weather as a trap signal against a favorite unless the opponent's offense is clearly better suited to the conditions (e.g. a dominant run game vs. a run defense that is actually poor in current-season data).
